title: Information-Theoretic Privacy Control for Sequential Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Sequential multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and enterprise decision-making, where multiple specialized agents collaboratively process a single user request. Although individual agents may satisfy local privacy constraints, sensitive information can still be inferred through sequential composition and intermediate representations. In this work, we study \emph{compositional privacy leakage} in sequential LLM agent pipelines. We formalize leakage using mutual information and derive a theoretical bound that characterizes how locally introduced leakage can amplify across agents under sequential execution. Motivated by this analysis, we propose a privacy-regularized training framework that directly constrains information flow between agent outputs and agent-local sensitive variables. We evaluate our approach across sequential agent pipelines of varying depth on three benchmark datasets, demonstrating stable optimization dynamics and consistent, interpretable privacy-utility trade-offs. Our results show that privacy in agentic LLM systems cannot be guaranteed by local constraints alone and must instead be treated as a system-level property during both training and deployment.

AI.tldr: Sequential LLM agent systems leak sensitive info through composition; paper formalizes compositional privacy leakage, proposes privacy-regularized training to constrain info flow between agents.
AI.motivation: Sequential multi-agent LLM systems in sensitive domains (healthcare, finance, enterprise) have privacy risks where local privacy constraints fail to prevent information leakage through sequential composition and intermediate representations.
AI.method: Formalizes compositional privacy leakage using mutual information, derives theoretical bound on leakage amplification across agents, proposes privacy-regularized training framework that directly constrains information flow between agent outputs and agent-local sensitive variables.
AI.result: Evaluated across sequential agent pipelines of varying depth on three benchmark datasets, showing stable optimization dynamics and consistent, interpretable privacy-utility trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Privacy in agentic LLM systems cannot be guaranteed by local constraints alone and must be treated as a system-level property during both training and deployment.

title: The Coordination Gap: Alternation Metrics for Temporal Dynamics in Multi-Agent Battle of the Exes
comment: 40 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to Mathematical Social Sciences
summary:
Multi-agent coordination dilemmas expose a fundamental tension between individual optimization and collective welfare, yet characterizing such coordination requires metrics sensitive to temporal structure and collective dynamics. As a diagnostic testbed, we study a BoE-derived multi-agent variant of the Battle of the Exes, formalizing it as a Markov game in which turn-taking emerges as a periodic coordination regime. Conventional outcome-based metrics (e.g., efficiency and min/max fairness) are temporally blind -- they cannot distinguish structured alternation from monopolistic or random access patterns -- and fairness ratios lose discriminative power as n grows, obscuring inequities.
  To address this limitation, we introduce Perfect Alternation (PA) as a reference coordination regime and propose six novel Alternation (ALT) metrics designed as temporally sensitive observables of coordination quality. Using Q-learning agents as a minimal adaptive diagnostic baseline, and comparing against random-policy null processes, we uncover a clear measurement failure: despite exhibiting deceptively high traditional metrics (e.g., reward fairness often exceeding 0.9), learned policies perform up to 81% below random baselines under ALT-variant evaluation -- a deficit already present in the two-agent case and intensifying as n grows.
  These results demonstrate, in this setting, that high aggregate payoffs can coexist with poor temporal coordination, and that conventional metrics may severely mischaracterize emergent dynamics. Our findings underscore the necessity of temporally aware observables for analyzing coordination in multi-agent games and highlight random-policy baselines as essential null processes for interpreting coordination outcomes relative to chance-level behavior.

AI.tldr: Traditional fairness metrics fail to detect poor temporal coordination in multi-agent games; new Alternation (ALT) metrics reveal learned policies perform up to 81% worse than random baselines despite high conventional scores.
AI.motivation: Conventional outcome-based metrics (efficiency, fairness ratios) are temporally blind and cannot distinguish structured coordination patterns from random or monopolistic access, especially as the number of agents grows, obscuring true coordination quality.
AI.method: Introduce Perfect Alternation (PA) as reference coordination regime; propose six novel Alternation (ALT) metrics as temporally sensitive observables; use Q-learning agents as adaptive diagnostic baseline; compare against random-policy null processes in a BoE-derived multi-agent Battle of the Exes Markov game.
AI.result: Learned policies show deceptively high traditional metrics (reward fairness often >0.9) but perform up to 81% below random baselines under ALT evaluation; deficit present in two-agent case and intensifies with more agents; high aggregate payoffs coexist with poor temporal coordination.
AI.conclusion: Conventional metrics severely mischaracterize emergent dynamics; temporally aware observables are necessary for analyzing coordination; random-policy baselines are essential null processes for interpreting coordination outcomes relative to chance-level behavior.

title: Evaluating LLM Alignment With Human Trust Models
comment: This paper will appear in the post-proceedings of ICAART 2026
summary: Trust plays a pivotal role in enabling effective cooperation, reducing uncertainty, and guiding decision-making in both human interactions and multi-agent systems. Although it is significant, there is limited understanding of how large language models (LLMs) internally conceptualize and reason about trust. This work presents a white-box analysis of trust representation in EleutherAI/gpt-j-6B, using contrastive prompting to generate embedding vectors within the activation space of the LLM for diadic trust and related interpersonal relationship attributes. We first identified trust-related concepts from five established human trust models. We then determined a threshold for significant conceptual alignment by computing pairwise cosine similarities across 60 general emotional concepts. Then we measured the cosine similarities between the LLM's internal representation of trust and the derived trust-related concepts. Our results show that the internal trust representation of EleutherAI/gpt-j-6B aligns most closely with the Castelfranchi socio-cognitive model, followed by the Marsh Model. These findings indicate that LLMs encode socio-cognitive constructs in their activation space in ways that support meaningful comparative analyses, inform theories of social cognition, and support the design of human-AI collaborative systems.

AI.tldr: White-box analysis reveals GPT-J-6B's internal trust representation aligns most with Castelfranchi socio-cognitive model, showing LLMs encode social constructs in activation space.
AI.motivation: Trust is crucial for cooperation and decision-making in multi-agent systems, but there's limited understanding of how LLMs internally conceptualize and reason about trust. The paper aims to analyze trust representation in LLMs using white-box methods.
AI.method: Used contrastive prompting to generate embedding vectors in GPT-J-6B's activation space for dyadic trust and interpersonal relationship attributes. Identified trust-related concepts from five established human trust models, established threshold for conceptual alignment using pairwise cosine similarities across 60 general emotional concepts, then measured similarities between LLM's trust representation and derived trust concepts.
AI.result: GPT-J-6B's internal trust representation aligns most closely with the Castelfranchi socio-cognitive model, followed by the Marsh Model. The LLM encodes socio-cognitive constructs in ways that support meaningful comparative analyses.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode socio-cognitive constructs in their activation space in ways that support comparative analyses, inform social cognition theories, and aid human-AI collaborative system design. The white-box approach provides insights into how LLMs internally represent complex social concepts like trust.

title: MASFactory: A Graph-centric Framework for Orchestrating LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems with Vibe Graphing
comment: Submitted to ACL 2026 Demo Track. 10 pages, 6 figures. Code and documentation are available at: https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/MASFactory
summary: Large language model-based (LLM-based) multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly used to extend agentic problem solving via role specialization and collaboration. MAS workflows can be naturally modeled as directed computation graphs, where nodes execute agents/sub-workflows and edges encode dependencies and message passing. However, implementing complex graph workflows in current frameworks still requires substantial manual effort, offers limited reuse, and makes it difficult to integrate heterogeneous external context sources. To overcome these limitations, we present MASFactory, a graph-centric framework for orchestrating LLM-based MAS. It introduces Vibe Graphing, a human-in-the-loop approach that compiles natural-language intent into an editable workflow specification and then into an executable graph. In addition, the framework provides reusable components and pluggable context integration, as well as a visualizer for topology preview, runtime tracing, and human-in-the-loop interaction. We evaluate MASFactory on seven public benchmarks, validating both reproduction consistency for representative MAS methods and the effectiveness of Vibe Graphing. Our code (https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/MASFactory) and video (https://youtu.be/ANynzVfY32k) are publicly available.

AI.tldr: MASFactory is a graph-centric framework for orchestrating LLM-based multi-agent systems that uses Vibe Graphing to compile natural-language intent into executable workflows, with reusable components and visual tools.
AI.motivation: Current frameworks for implementing complex graph workflows in LLM-based multi-agent systems require substantial manual effort, offer limited reuse, and make it difficult to integrate heterogeneous external context sources.
AI.method: MASFactory introduces Vibe Graphing, a human-in-the-loop approach that compiles natural-language intent into an editable workflow specification and then into an executable graph. The framework provides reusable components, pluggable context integration, and a visualizer for topology preview, runtime tracing, and human-in-the-loop interaction.
AI.result: The framework was evaluated on seven public benchmarks, validating both reproduction consistency for representative MAS methods and the effectiveness of Vibe Graphing. Code and video demonstrations are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: MASFactory addresses limitations in current multi-agent system frameworks by providing a graph-centric approach with natural-language workflow specification, reusable components, and integrated visualization tools for more efficient LLM-based multi-agent system development.

title: RoboLayout: Differentiable 3D Scene Generation for Embodied Agents
summary: Recent advances in vision language models (VLMs) have shown strong potential for spatial reasoning and 3D scene layout generation from open-ended language instructions. However, generating layouts that are not only semantically coherent but also feasible for interaction by embodied agents remains challenging, particularly in physically constrained indoor environments. In this paper, RoboLayout is introduced as an extension of LayoutVLM that augments the original framework with agent-aware reasoning and improved optimization stability. RoboLayout integrates explicit reachability constraints into a differentiable layout optimization process, enabling the generation of layouts that are navigable and actionable by embodied agents. Importantly, the agent abstraction is not limited to a specific robot platform and can represent diverse entities with distinct physical capabilities, such as service robots, warehouse robots, humans of different age groups, or animals, allowing environment design to be tailored to the intended agent. In addition, a local refinement stage is proposed that selectively reoptimizes problematic object placements while keeping the remainder of the scene fixed, improving convergence efficiency without increasing global optimization iterations. Overall, RoboLayout preserves the strong semantic alignment and physical plausibility of LayoutVLM while enhancing applicability to agent-centric indoor scene generation, as demonstrated by experimental results across diverse scene configurations.

AI.tldr: RoboLayout extends LayoutVLM to generate physically feasible indoor scene layouts for diverse embodied agents by integrating reachability constraints and local refinement optimization.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs generate semantically coherent layouts but lack consideration for physical feasibility and agent interaction capabilities, especially in constrained indoor environments where layouts must be navigable and actionable by embodied agents.
AI.method: Extends LayoutVLM with agent-aware reasoning and improved optimization stability by: 1) Integrating explicit reachability constraints into differentiable layout optimization, 2) Supporting diverse agent abstractions (robots, humans, animals), 3) Adding local refinement stage that selectively reoptimizes problematic object placements while keeping rest of scene fixed.
AI.result: RoboLayout preserves LayoutVLM's semantic alignment and physical plausibility while enhancing applicability to agent-centric indoor scene generation, demonstrated across diverse scene configurations with improved convergence efficiency.
AI.conclusion: RoboLayout successfully bridges the gap between semantic scene understanding and physical feasibility for embodied agents, enabling tailored environment design for diverse agent types while maintaining optimization efficiency through local refinement.

title: Verify as You Go: An LLM-Powered Browser Extension for Fake News Detection
summary: The rampant spread of fake news in the digital age poses serious risks to public trust and democratic institutions, underscoring the need for effective, transparent, and user-centered detection tools. Existing browser extensions often fall short due to opaque model behavior, limited explanatory support, and a lack of meaningful user engagement. This paper introduces Aletheia, a novel browser extension that leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Large Language Models (LLMs) to detect fake news and provide evidence-based explanations. Aletheia further includes two interactive components: a Discussion Hub that enables user dialogue around flagged content and a Stay Informed feature that surfaces recent fact-checks. Through extensive experiments, we show that Aletheia outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in detection performance. Complementing this empirical evaluation, a complementary user study with 250 participants confirms the system's usability and perceived effectiveness, highlighting its potential as a transparent tool for combating online fake news.

AI.tldr: Aletheia is a browser extension using RAG and LLMs to detect fake news with evidence-based explanations, interactive discussion features, and outperforms existing methods.
AI.motivation: Fake news proliferation threatens public trust and democracy; current browser extensions are inadequate due to opaque models, poor explanations, and lack of user engagement.
AI.method: Aletheia combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Large Language Models (LLMs) for fake news detection, provides evidence-based explanations, and includes Discussion Hub for user dialogue and Stay Informed feature for recent fact-checks.
AI.result: Aletheia outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in detection performance; user study with 250 participants confirms system usability and perceived effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Aletheia represents a transparent, effective tool for combating online fake news through advanced AI detection, explanatory transparency, and user engagement features.

title: Conversational Demand Response: Bidirectional Aggregator-Prosumer Coordination through Agentic AI
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Code available at: https://github.com/RedaElMakroum/cdr
summary: Residential demand response depends on sustained prosumer participation, yet existing coordination is either fully automated, or limited to one-way dispatch signals and price alerts that offer little possibility for informed decision-making. This paper introduces Conversational Demand Response (CDR), a coordination mechanism where aggregators and prosumers interact through bidirectional natural language, enabled through agentic AI. A two-tier multi-agent architecture is developed in which an aggregator agent dispatches flexibility requests and a prosumer Home Energy Management System (HEMS) assesses deliverability and cost-benefit by calling an optimization-based tool. CDR also enables prosumer-initiated upstream communication, where changes in preferences can reach the aggregator directly. Proof-of-concept evaluation shows that interactions complete in under 12 seconds. The architecture illustrates how agentic AI can bridge the aggregator-prosumer coordination gap, providing the scalability of automated DR while preserving the transparency, explainability, and user agency necessary for sustained prosumer participation. All system components, including agent prompts, orchestration logic, and simulation interfaces, are released as open source to enable reproducibility and further development.

AI.tldr: CDR uses bidirectional natural language conversations between aggregators and prosumers via agentic AI to coordinate demand response, balancing automation with user agency.
AI.motivation: Existing demand response coordination is either fully automated (lacking transparency) or limited to one-way signals (offering little decision-making capability), creating a gap between scalability and user participation.
AI.method: Two-tier multi-agent architecture with aggregator agents dispatching flexibility requests and prosumer HEMS agents assessing deliverability via optimization tools, enabling bidirectional natural language communication and prosumer-initiated upstream feedback.
AI.result: Proof-of-concept evaluation shows interactions complete in under 12 seconds, demonstrating feasibility. System components released as open source for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: CDR bridges the aggregator-prosumer coordination gap using agentic AI, providing automated DR scalability while preserving transparency, explainability, and user agency necessary for sustained prosumer participation.

title: Real-Time AI Service Economy: A Framework for Agentic Computing Across the Continuum
summary: Real-time AI services increasingly operate across the device-edge-cloud continuum, where autonomous AI agents generate latency-sensitive workloads, orchestrate multi-stage processing pipelines, and compete for shared resources under policy and governance constraints. This article shows that the structure of service-dependency graphs, modelled as DAGs whose nodes represent compute stages and whose edges encode execution ordering, is a primary determinant of whether decentralised, price-based resource allocation can work reliably at scale. When dependency graphs are hierarchical (tree or series-parallel), prices converge to stable equilibria, optimal allocations can be computed efficiently, and under appropriate mechanism design (with quasilinear utilities and discrete slice items), agents have no incentive to misreport their valuations within each decision epoch. When dependencies are more complex, with cross-cutting ties between pipeline stages, prices oscillate, allocation quality degrades, and the system becomes difficult to manage. To bridge this gap, we propose a hybrid management architecture in which cross-domain integrators encapsulate complex sub-graphs into resource slices that present a simpler, well-structured interface to the rest of the market. A systematic ablation study across six experiments (1,620 runs, 10 seeds each) confirms that (i) dependency-graph topology is a first-order determinant of price stability and scalability,(ii) the hybrid architecture reduces price volatility by up to 70-75% without sacrificing throughput, (iii) governance constraints create quantifiable efficiency-compliance trade-offs that depend jointly on topology and load, and (iv) under truthful bidding the decentralised market matches a centralised value-optimal baseline, confirming that decentralised coordination can replicate centralised allocation quality.

AI.tldr: Dependency graph topology determines viability of decentralized price-based resource allocation in AI continuum; hierarchical graphs enable stable equilibria while complex graphs cause instability, addressed via hybrid architecture with cross-domain integrators.
AI.motivation: Real-time AI services operate across device-edge-cloud continuum with latency-sensitive workloads, multi-stage pipelines, and resource competition under governance constraints. Need to understand when decentralized, price-based resource allocation can work reliably at scale.
AI.method: Model service-dependency graphs as DAGs where nodes are compute stages and edges encode execution ordering. Analyze how graph topology affects price stability. Propose hybrid architecture where cross-domain integrators encapsulate complex sub-graphs into resource slices with simpler interfaces. Conduct systematic ablation study across six experiments (1,620 runs, 10 seeds each).
AI.result: 1) Dependency-graph topology is primary determinant of price stability and scalability. 2) Hierarchical graphs (tree/series-parallel) enable price convergence to stable equilibria, efficient optimal allocation computation, and truthful bidding incentives. 3) Complex graphs with cross-cutting ties cause price oscillation and allocation degradation. 4) Hybrid architecture reduces price volatility by 70-75% without throughput sacrifice. 5) Governance constraints create quantifiable efficiency-compliance trade-offs dependent on topology and load. 6) Under truthful bidding, decentralized market matches centralized value-optimal baseline.
AI.conclusion: Dependency graph structure fundamentally determines viability of decentralized price-based resource allocation in AI continuum. Hierarchical graphs enable reliable decentralized coordination, while complex graphs require hybrid management with cross-domain integrators to maintain stability. Decentralized coordination can achieve centralized allocation quality when properly structured.

title: Attention Meets Reachability: Structural Equivalence and Efficiency in Grammar-Constrained LLM Decoding
summary: We study grammar-constrained decoding (GCD) as a coupling between an autoregressive next-token distribution and a reachability oracle over a pushdown system compiled from a context-free grammar (CFG). We prove an oracle invariance theorem: language-equivalent grammars induce identical admissible next-token sets for every prefix, hence identical logit masks, yet can yield provably different compiled state spaces and online ambiguity costs. We give exact control-state blowup counts for the canonical $a^n b^n$ language under redundant nonterminal delegation, and introduce a left-to-right structural ambiguity cost (SAC) measuring incremental packed-parse-forest growth per token. For two equivalent grammars over all finite strings, SAC is $O(1)$ per token under right-recursion but $Θ(t^2)$ per token and $Θ(n^3)$ cumulatively under concatenation. We establish engine-independent lower bounds: any sound, retrieval-efficient, parse-preserving online masking engine must incur $Ω(t^2)$ work per token on a specific constant-size CFG family, unconditionally within this model. We define decoding-cost equivalence classes of grammars and prove existence of minimal-SAC representatives within bounded rewrite families. Finally, we characterize the true conditional sampler via a Doob $h$-transform and derive sharp one-step KL and total-variation distortion bounds for hard-masked decoding in terms of survival-probability spread among admissible next tokens. We integrate these results with Transformer and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, derive latency envelopes in terms of vocabulary size, active state sets, and beam width, and connect SAC to instrumentation-based predictive performance models and automated grammar optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper studies grammar-constrained decoding (GCD) as coupling between autoregressive language models and pushdown systems from CFGs, proving oracle invariance, analyzing structural ambiguity costs, establishing lower bounds for online masking engines, and deriving distortion bounds for hard-masked decoding.
AI.motivation: To understand the computational and performance implications of grammar-constrained decoding when different but language-equivalent grammars are used, particularly focusing on how grammar structure affects decoding efficiency, ambiguity costs, and sampling quality.
AI.method: Formal analysis of GCD as coupling between autoregressive models and pushdown automata from CFGs, proving oracle invariance theorem, analyzing structural ambiguity cost (SAC), establishing lower bounds for online masking engines, defining grammar equivalence classes, deriving distortion bounds via Doob h-transform, and integration with Transformer/MoE architectures.
AI.result: Proved oracle invariance: language-equivalent grammars yield identical logit masks but different state spaces and ambiguity costs. Showed SAC is O(1) under right-recursion but Θ(t²) per token under concatenation. Established Ω(t²) lower bound for online masking engines. Derived sharp KL and total-variation bounds for hard-masked decoding. Integrated results with modern architectures and latency models.
AI.conclusion: Grammar structure significantly impacts decoding efficiency despite language equivalence, with right-recursive grammars offering optimal SAC. The analysis provides theoretical foundations for grammar optimization in GCD, establishes fundamental lower bounds, and offers distortion guarantees for practical implementations with modern neural architectures.

title: Talk Freely, Execute Strictly: Schema-Gated Agentic AI for Flexible and Reproducible Scientific Workflows
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) can now translate a researcher's plain-language goal into executable computation, yet scientific workflows demand determinism, provenance, and governance that are difficult to guarantee when an LLM decides what runs. Semi-structured interviews with 18 experts across 10 industrial R&D stakeholders surface 2 competing requirements--deterministic, constrained execution and conversational flexibility without workflow rigidity--together with boundary properties (human-in-the-loop control and transparency) that any resolution must satisfy. We propose schema-gated orchestration as the resolving principle: the schema becomes a mandatory execution boundary at the composed-workflow level, so that nothing runs unless the complete action--including cross-step dependencies--validates against a machine-checkable specification.
  We operationalize the 2 requirements as execution determinism (ED) and conversational flexibility (CF), and use these axes to review 20 systems spanning 5 architectural groups along a validation-scope spectrum. Scores are assigned via a multi-model protocol--15 independent sessions across 3 LLM families--yielding substantial-to-near-perfect inter-model agreement (Krippendorff a=0.80 for ED and a=0.98 for CF), demonstrating that multi-model LLM scoring can serve as a reusable alternative to human expert panels for architectural assessment.
  The resulting landscape reveals an empirical Pareto front--no reviewed system achieves both high flexibility and high determinism--but a convergence zone emerges between the generative and workflow-centric extremes. We argue that a schema-gated architecture, separating conversational from execution authority, is positioned to decouple this trade-off, and distill 3 operational principles--clarification-before-execution, constrained plan-act orchestration, and tool-to-workflow-level gating--to guide adoption.

AI.tldr: Schema-gated orchestration resolves tension between deterministic execution and conversational flexibility in LLM-driven scientific workflows by using schemas as mandatory execution boundaries that validate complete actions before running.
AI.motivation: Scientific workflows require determinism, provenance, and governance that are difficult to guarantee when LLMs decide what runs, creating tension between constrained execution and conversational flexibility without workflow rigidity.
AI.method: Proposed schema-gated orchestration with schemas as mandatory execution boundaries; operationalized requirements as execution determinism (ED) and conversational flexibility (CF); reviewed 20 systems across 5 architectural groups using multi-model LLM scoring protocol (15 sessions across 3 LLM families).
AI.result: Multi-model LLM scoring showed substantial-to-near-perfect inter-model agreement (α=0.80 for ED, α=0.98 for CF); revealed empirical Pareto front showing no system achieves both high flexibility and high determinism; identified convergence zone between generative and workflow-centric extremes.
AI.conclusion: Schema-gated architecture separating conversational from execution authority can decouple the flexibility-determinism trade-off; distilled three operational principles: clarification-before-execution, constrained plan-act orchestration, and tool-to-workflow-level gating.

title: Reasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting misbehaviors and understanding the motivations of modern reasoning models. However, if models can control what they verbalize in their CoT, it could undermine CoT monitorability. To measure this undesirable capability -- CoT controllability -- we introduce the CoT-Control evaluation suite, which includes tasks that require models to solve problems while adhering to CoT instructions, e.g., reasoning about a genetics question without using the word 'chromosome'. We show that reasoning models possess significantly lower CoT controllability than output controllability; for instance, Claude Sonnet 4.5 can control its CoT only 2.7% of the time but 61.9% when controlling its final output. We also find that CoT controllability is higher for larger models and decreases with more RL training, test-time compute, and increased problem difficulty. CoT controllability failures extend even to situations in which models are given incentives (as opposed to direct requests) to evade CoT monitors, although models exhibit slightly higher controllability when they are told they are being monitored. Similarly, eliciting controllability by adversarially optimizing prompts does not meaningfully increase controllability. Our results leave us cautiously optimistic that CoT controllability is currently unlikely to be a failure mode of CoT monitorability. However, the mechanism behind low controllability is not well understood. Given its importance for maintaining CoT monitorability, we recommend that frontier labs track CoT controllability in future models.

AI.tldr: Chain-of-thought controllability is currently low in reasoning models, making CoT monitoring robust against evasion attempts, though frontier labs should track this capability in future models.
AI.motivation: To assess whether models can control what they verbalize in their chain-of-thought reasoning, which could undermine the monitorability and trustworthiness of CoT-based oversight systems.
AI.method: Introduced CoT-Control evaluation suite with tasks requiring models to solve problems while adhering to specific CoT instructions (e.g., reasoning without using certain words). Measured controllability across different models, training regimes, and conditions including incentives, monitoring awareness, and adversarial prompt optimization.
AI.result: Models show significantly lower CoT controllability than output controllability (Claude Sonnet 4.5: 2.7% vs 61.9%). Controllability increases with model size but decreases with more RL training, test-time compute, and problem difficulty. Models struggle even with incentives to evade monitors, though controllability slightly improves when aware of monitoring. Adversarial prompting doesn't meaningfully increase controllability.
AI.conclusion: Current CoT controllability is low, suggesting CoT monitorability is robust for now. However, the underlying mechanism is not well understood, and frontier labs should track this capability in future models to maintain monitorability as models evolve.

title: NOTAI.AI: Explainable Detection of Machine-Generated Text via Curvature and Feature Attribution
summary: We present NOTAI.AI, an explainable framework for machine-generated text detection that extends Fast-DetectGPT by integrating curvature-based signals with neural and stylometric features in a supervised setting. The system combines 17 interpretable features, including Conditional Probability Curvature, ModernBERT detector score, readability metrics, and stylometric cues, within a gradient-boosted tree (XGBoost) meta-classifier to determine whether a text is human- or AI-generated. Furthermore, NOTAI.AI applies Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) to provide both local and global feature-level attribution. These attributions are further translated into structured natural-language rationales through an LLM-based explanation layer, which enables user-facing interpretability. The system is deployed as an interactive web application that supports real-time analysis, visual feature inspection, and structured evidence presentation. A web interface allows users to input text and inspect how neural and statistical signals influence the final decision. The source code and demo video are publicly available to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: NOTAI.AI is an explainable framework for AI-generated text detection that combines curvature-based signals with neural and stylometric features using XGBoost, with SHAP-based explanations and an LLM explanation layer for interpretability.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the need for explainable AI-generated text detection systems that go beyond black-box approaches by providing interpretable features and structured explanations for detection decisions.
AI.method: Extends Fast-DetectGPT by integrating curvature-based signals with neural and stylometric features (17 total features including Conditional Probability Curvature, ModernBERT detector score, readability metrics, and stylometric cues) in a supervised XGBoost meta-classifier, with SHAP for feature attribution and an LLM-based explanation layer for natural-language rationales.
AI.result: Developed an interactive web application supporting real-time analysis, visual feature inspection, and structured evidence presentation, with publicly available source code and demo video for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: NOTAI.AI provides an explainable framework for AI-generated text detection that combines multiple signal types with interpretable explanations, enabling better understanding of detection decisions through both technical feature analysis and user-friendly natural language rationales.

title: Evolving Medical Imaging Agents via Experience-driven Self-skill Discovery
summary: Clinical image interpretation is inherently multi-step and tool-centric: clinicians iteratively combine visual evidence with patient context, quantify findings, and refine their decisions through a sequence of specialized procedures. While LLM-based agents promise to orchestrate such heterogeneous medical tools, existing systems treat tool sets and invocation strategies as static after deployment. This design is brittle under real-world domain shifts, across tasks, and evolving diagnostic requirements, where predefined tool chains frequently degrade and demand costly manual re-design. We propose MACRO, a self-evolving, experience-augmented medical agent that shifts from static tool composition to experience-driven tool discovery. From verified execution trajectories, the agent autonomously identifies recurring effective multi-step tool sequences, synthesizes them into reusable composite tools, and registers these as new high-level primitives that continuously expand its behavioral repertoire. A lightweight image-feature memory grounds tool selection in a visual-clinical context, while a GRPO-like training loop reinforces reliable invocation of discovered composites, enabling closed-loop self-improvement with minimal supervision. Extensive experiments across diverse medical imaging datasets and tasks demonstrate that autonomous composite tool discovery consistently improves multi-step orchestration accuracy and cross-domain generalization over strong baselines and recent state-of-the-art agentic methods, bridging the gap between brittle static tool use and adaptive, context-aware clinical AI assistance. Code will be available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: MACRO is a self-evolving medical AI agent that autonomously discovers and synthesizes effective multi-step tool sequences from execution experience, creating reusable composite tools to improve orchestration accuracy and cross-domain generalization in clinical image interpretation.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based medical agents use static tool sets and invocation strategies that become brittle under real-world domain shifts, evolving diagnostic requirements, and across different tasks, requiring costly manual redesign when predefined tool chains degrade.
AI.method: MACRO autonomously identifies recurring effective multi-step tool sequences from verified execution trajectories, synthesizes them into reusable composite tools, and registers these as new high-level primitives. It uses a lightweight image-feature memory to ground tool selection in visual-clinical context and employs a GRPO-like training loop to reinforce reliable invocation of discovered composites for closed-loop self-improvement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse medical imaging datasets and tasks demonstrate that autonomous composite tool discovery consistently improves multi-step orchestration accuracy and cross-domain generalization over strong baselines and recent state-of-the-art agentic methods.
AI.conclusion: MACRO bridges the gap between brittle static tool use and adaptive, context-aware clinical AI assistance by shifting from static tool composition to experience-driven tool discovery, enabling continuous expansion of behavioral repertoire with minimal supervision.

title: Safer Reasoning Traces: Measuring and Mitigating Chain-of-Thought Leakage in LLMs
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves LLM reasoning but can increase privacy risk by resurfacing personally identifiable information (PII) from the prompt into reasoning traces and outputs, even under policies that instruct the model not to restate PII. We study such direct, inference-time PII leakage using a model-agnostic framework that (i) defines leakage as risk-weighted, token-level events across 11 PII types, (ii) traces leakage curves as a function of the allowed CoT budget, and (iii) compares open- and closed-source model families on a structured PII dataset with a hierarchical risk taxonomy. We find that CoT consistently elevates leakage, especially for high-risk categories, and that leakage is strongly family- and budget-dependent. Increasing the reasoning budget can either amplify or attenuate leakage depending on the base model. We then benchmark lightweight inference-time gatekeepers: a rule-based detector, a TF-IDF + logistic regression classifier, a GLiNER-based NER model, and an LLM-as-judge, using risk-weighted F1, Macro-F1, and recall. No single method dominates across models or budgets, motivating hybrid, style-adaptive gatekeeping policies that balance utility and risk under a common, reproducible protocol.

AI.tldr: CoT prompting increases PII leakage risk in LLMs, with leakage patterns varying by model family and reasoning budget; no single detection method dominates, requiring hybrid gatekeeping approaches.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought prompting improves reasoning but increases privacy risks by causing PII from prompts to resurface in reasoning traces and outputs, even when models are instructed not to restate PII.
AI.method: Developed a model-agnostic framework to measure direct inference-time PII leakage: (1) defines leakage as risk-weighted token-level events across 11 PII types, (2) traces leakage curves as function of CoT budget, (3) compares open- and closed-source models on structured PII dataset with hierarchical risk taxonomy, and (4) benchmarks lightweight inference-time gatekeepers including rule-based detector, TF-IDF+logistic regression, GLiNER-based NER, and LLM-as-judge.
AI.result: CoT consistently elevates PII leakage, especially for high-risk categories; leakage is strongly dependent on model family and reasoning budget; increasing reasoning budget can either amplify or attenuate leakage depending on base model; no single gatekeeping method dominates across models or budgets.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid, style-adaptive gatekeeping policies are needed to balance utility and risk under a common, reproducible protocol, as PII leakage patterns vary significantly across models and reasoning budgets.

title: The World Won't Stay Still: Programmable Evolution for Agent Benchmarks
summary: LLM-powered agents fulfill user requests by interacting with environments, querying data, and invoking tools in a multi-turn process. Yet, most existing benchmarks assume static environments with fixed schemas and toolsets, neglecting the evolutionary nature of the real world and agents' robustness to environmental changes. In this paper, we study a crucial problem: how to evolve the agent environment in a scalable and controllable way, thereby better evaluating agents' adaptability to real-world dynamics. We propose ProEvolve, a graph-based framework that makes environment evolution programmable. At its core, a typed relational graph provides a unified, explicit representation of the environment: data, tools, and schema. Under this formalism, adding, removing, or modifying capabilities are expressed as graph transformations that coherently propagate updates across tools, schemas, and data access. Building on this, ProEvolve can (1) program the evolutionary dynamics as graph transformations to generate environments automatically, and (2) instantiate task sandboxes via subgraph sampling and programming. We validate ProEvolve by evolving a single environment into 200 environments and 3,000 task sandboxes, and benchmark representative agents accordingly.

AI.tldr: ProEvolve is a graph-based framework for programmatically evolving LLM agent environments to evaluate agent adaptability to real-world dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assume static environments with fixed schemas and toolsets, neglecting the evolutionary nature of real-world environments and agents' robustness to environmental changes.
AI.method: ProEvolve uses a typed relational graph as a unified representation of environment data, tools, and schema. Environment evolution is expressed as graph transformations that coherently propagate updates across tools, schemas, and data access.
AI.result: The framework successfully evolved a single environment into 200 environments and 3,000 task sandboxes, enabling comprehensive benchmarking of representative agents' adaptability.
AI.conclusion: ProEvolve provides a scalable and controllable approach to environment evolution, addressing the gap in evaluating LLM-powered agents' adaptability to real-world dynamics.

title: The Fragility Of Moral Judgment In Large Language Models
summary:
People increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for everyday moral and interpersonal guidance, yet these systems cannot interrogate missing context and judge dilemmas as presented. We introduce a perturbation framework for testing the stability and manipulability of LLM moral judgments while holding the underlying moral conflict constant. Using 2,939 dilemmas from r/AmItheAsshole (January-March 2025), we generate three families of content perturbations: surface edits (lexical/structural noise), point-of-view shifts (voice and stance neutralization), and persuasion cues (self-positioning, social proof, pattern admissions, victim framing). We also vary the evaluation protocol (output ordering, instruction placement, and unstructured prompting). We evaluated all variants with four models (GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3, Qwen2.5-72B) (N=129,156 judgments).
  Surface perturbations produce low flip rates (7.5%), largely within the self-consistency noise floor (4-13%), whereas point-of-view shifts induce substantially higher instability (24.3%). A large subset of dilemmas (37.9%) is robust to surface noise yet flips under perspective changes, indicating that models condition on narrative voice as a pragmatic cue. Instability concentrates in morally ambiguous cases; scenarios where no party is assigned blame are most susceptible. Persuasion perturbations yield systematic directional shifts. Protocol choices dominate all other factors: agreement between structured protocols is only 67.6% (kappa=0.55), and only 35.7% of model-scenario units match across all three protocols. These results show that LLM moral judgments are co-produced by narrative form and task scaffolding, raising reproducibility and equity concerns when outcomes depend on presentation skill rather than moral substance.

AI.tldr: LLM moral judgments are highly sensitive to narrative framing and evaluation protocols, with perspective shifts causing 24.3% judgment flips and protocol choices dominating all other factors in determining outcomes.
AI.motivation: People increasingly use LLMs for moral guidance, but these systems cannot interrogate missing context or judge dilemmas as presented, raising concerns about stability and manipulability of their moral judgments.
AI.method: Developed a perturbation framework using 2,939 dilemmas from r/AmItheAsshole, generating three families of content perturbations (surface edits, point-of-view shifts, persuasion cues) and varying evaluation protocols, testing four LLMs with 129,156 judgments.
AI.result: Surface perturbations produced low flip rates (7.5%), point-of-view shifts caused high instability (24.3%), 37.9% of dilemmas were robust to surface noise but flipped under perspective changes, and protocol choices dominated all factors with only 35.7% consistency across protocols.
AI.conclusion: LLM moral judgments are co-produced by narrative form and task scaffolding, raising reproducibility and equity concerns when outcomes depend on presentation skill rather than moral substance.

title: DeepFact: Co-Evolving Benchmarks and Agents for Deep Research Factuality
summary: Search-augmented LLM agents can produce deep research reports (DRRs), but verifying claim-level factuality remains challenging. Existing fact-checkers are primarily designed for general-domain, factoid-style atomic claims, and there is no benchmark to test whether such verifiers transfer to DRRs. Yet building such a benchmark is itself difficult. We first show that static expert-labeled benchmarks are brittle in this setting: in a controlled study with PhD-level specialists, unassisted experts achieve only 60.8% accuracy on a hidden micro-gold set of verifiable claims. We propose Evolving Benchmarking via Audit-then-Score (AtS), where benchmark labels and rationales are explicitly revisable: when a verifier disagrees with the current benchmark, it must submit evidence; an auditor adjudicates the dispute; and accepted revisions update the benchmark before models are scored. Across four AtS rounds, expert micro-gold accuracy rises to 90.9%, indicating experts are substantially more reliable as auditors than as one-shot labelers. We instantiate AtS as DeepFact-Bench, a versioned DRR factuality benchmark with auditable rationales, and DeepFact-Eval, a document-level verification agent (with a grouped lite variant) that outperforms existing verifiers on DeepFact-Bench and transfers well to external factuality datasets.

AI.tldr: Evolving Benchmarking via Audit-then-Score (AtS) addresses challenges in verifying claim-level factuality in deep research reports by creating revisable benchmarks where verifiers can submit evidence for disputed labels, with auditors adjudicating to improve benchmark quality.
AI.motivation: Existing fact-checkers are designed for general-domain atomic claims and don't transfer well to deep research reports (DRRs). Static expert-labeled benchmarks are brittle, with experts achieving only 60.8% accuracy on hidden micro-gold sets, highlighting the need for more reliable verification methods for complex research content.
AI.method: Proposes Evolving Benchmarking via Audit-then-Score (AtS): 1) When a verifier disagrees with benchmark labels, it submits evidence; 2) An auditor adjudicates the dispute; 3) Accepted revisions update the benchmark before models are scored. This creates versioned benchmarks with auditable rationales. Instantiated as DeepFact-Bench (benchmark) and DeepFact-Eval (verification agent with grouped lite variant).
AI.result: Across four AtS rounds, expert micro-gold accuracy rose from 60.8% to 90.9%, showing experts are substantially more reliable as auditors than one-shot labelers. DeepFact-Eval outperforms existing verifiers on DeepFact-Bench and transfers well to external factuality datasets.
AI.conclusion: AtS framework enables creation of high-quality, revisable benchmarks for DRR factuality verification. The approach demonstrates that experts serve better as auditors in iterative processes than as one-shot labelers, and the resulting DeepFact-Eval agent shows strong performance and transferability.

title: FreeTxt-Vi: A Benchmarked Vietnamese-English Toolkit for Segmentation, Sentiment, and Summarisation
summary: FreeTxt-Vi is a free and open source web based toolkit for creating and analysing bilingual Vietnamese English text collections. Positioned at the intersection of corpus linguistics and natural language processing NLP it enables users to build explore and interpret free text data without requiring programming expertise. The system combines corpus analysis features such as concordancing keyword analysis word relation exploration and interactive visualisation with transformer based NLP components for sentiment analysis and summarisation. A key contribution of this work is the design of a unified bilingual NLP pipeline that integrates a hybrid VnCoreNLP and Byte Pair Encoding BPE segmentation strategy a fine tuned TabularisAI sentiment classifier and a fine tuned Qwen2.5 model for abstractive summarisation. Unlike existing text analysis platforms FreeTxt Vi is evaluated as a set of language processing components. We conduct a three part evaluation covering segmentation sentiment analysis and summarisation and show that our approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to widely used baselines in both Vietnamese and English. By reducing technical barriers to multilingual text analysis FreeTxt Vi supports reproducible research and promotes the development of language resources for Vietnamese a widely spoken but underrepresented language in NLP. The toolkit is applicable to domains including education digital humanities cultural heritage and the social sciences where qualitative text data are common but often difficult to process at scale.

AI.tldr: FreeTxt-Vi is an open-source web toolkit for bilingual Vietnamese-English text analysis that combines corpus linguistics features with transformer-based NLP, featuring a unified bilingual pipeline with hybrid segmentation, sentiment classification, and summarization models.
AI.motivation: To create an accessible tool that reduces technical barriers for multilingual text analysis, particularly for Vietnamese (a widely spoken but underrepresented language in NLP), supporting reproducible research and promoting language resource development for domains like education, digital humanities, and social sciences.
AI.method: Develops a web-based toolkit integrating corpus analysis features (concordancing, keyword analysis, word relation exploration, visualization) with transformer-based NLP components. Implements a unified bilingual pipeline with: 1) hybrid VnCoreNLP and Byte Pair Encoding segmentation strategy, 2) fine-tuned TabularisAI sentiment classifier, and 3) fine-tuned Qwen2.5 model for abstractive summarization.
AI.result: The system achieves competitive or superior performance compared to widely used baselines in both Vietnamese and English across three evaluation areas: segmentation, sentiment analysis, and summarization. The toolkit enables non-programmers to build, explore, and interpret bilingual text collections.
AI.conclusion: FreeTxt-Vi successfully bridges corpus linguistics and NLP, providing an accessible platform for bilingual Vietnamese-English text analysis that supports reproducible research and addresses the underrepresentation of Vietnamese in NLP resources, with applications across multiple academic and cultural domains.

title: An Interactive Multi-Agent System for Evaluation of New Product Concepts
comment: 46 pages, 3 figures + This paper proposes an LLM-based multi-agent system (MAS) for automated evaluation of new product concepts, incorporating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and cross-functional virtual agents to assess technical and market feasibility
summary: Product concept evaluation is a critical stage that determines strategic resource allocation and project success in enterprises. However, traditional expert-led approaches face limitations such as subjective bias and high time and cost requirements. To support this process, this study proposes an automated approach utilizing a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent system (MAS). Through a systematic analysis of previous research on product development and team collaboration, this study established two primary evaluation dimensions, namely technical feasibility and market feasibility. The proposed system consists of a team of eight virtual agents representing specialized domains such as R&D and marketing. These agents use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and real-time search tools to gather objective evidence and validate concepts through structured deliberations based on the established criteria. The agents were further fine-tuned using professional product review data to enhance their judgment accuracy. A case study involving professional display monitor concepts demonstrated that the system's evaluation rankings were consistent with those of senior industry experts. These results confirm the usability of the proposed multi-agent-based evaluation approach for supporting product development decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an LLM-based multi-agent system for automated product concept evaluation, addressing limitations of traditional expert-led approaches through objective evidence gathering and structured deliberations across technical and market feasibility dimensions.
AI.motivation: Traditional expert-led product concept evaluation suffers from subjective bias, high time requirements, and significant costs. There's a need for automated approaches that can provide objective, evidence-based evaluations to support strategic resource allocation decisions in enterprises.
AI.method: Developed an LLM-based multi-agent system with eight virtual agents representing specialized domains (R&D, marketing, etc.). Used retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and real-time search tools for objective evidence gathering. Fine-tuned agents with professional product review data. Structured deliberations based on two evaluation dimensions: technical feasibility and market feasibility.
AI.result: The system's evaluation rankings for professional display monitor concepts showed consistency with senior industry experts' rankings, demonstrating the system's practical usability and reliability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent-based evaluation approach is usable for supporting product development decisions, offering an automated alternative to traditional expert-led methods with reduced subjectivity and improved efficiency.

title: Towards Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation Based on Knowledge Graph: A Comparative Analysis
comment: The paper is 6 pages long and includes 5 figures and 3 tables illustrating the experimental framework and results. It is submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC 2025) and studies improving the robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems using knowledge graph based GraphRAG approaches
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was introduced to enhance the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) beyond their encoded prior knowledge. This is achieved by providing LLMs with an external source of knowledge, which helps reduce factual hallucinations and enables access to new information not available during pretraining. However, inconsistent retrieved information can negatively affect LLM responses. The Retrieval-Augmented Generation Benchmark (RGB) was introduced to evaluate the robustness of RAG systems under such conditions. In this work, we use the RGB corpus to evaluate LLMs in four scenarios: noise robustness, information integration, negative rejection, and counterfactual robustness. We perform a comparative analysis between the RGB RAG baseline and GraphRAG, a knowledge graph based retrieval system. We test three GraphRAG customizations to improve robustness. Results show improvements over the RGB baseline and provide insights for designing more reliable RAG systems for real world scenarios.

AI.tldr: GraphRAG outperforms baseline RAG systems on RGB benchmark across noise robustness, information integration, negative rejection, and counterfactual robustness scenarios through knowledge graph-based retrieval and customizations.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG systems struggle with inconsistent retrieved information that negatively impacts LLM responses, creating a need for more robust retrieval-augmented generation systems that can handle noisy, contradictory, or counterfactual information.
AI.method: Comparative analysis between RGB RAG baseline and GraphRAG (knowledge graph-based retrieval system) using RGB benchmark corpus. Evaluated four scenarios: noise robustness, information integration, negative rejection, and counterfactual robustness. Tested three GraphRAG customizations to improve robustness.
AI.result: GraphRAG with customizations shows improvements over RGB baseline across all four evaluation scenarios, demonstrating enhanced robustness to inconsistent retrieved information.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge graph-based retrieval systems like GraphRAG with appropriate customizations can create more reliable RAG systems for real-world applications by better handling inconsistent information scenarios.

title: Agentic LLM Planning via Step-Wise PDDL Simulation: An Empirical Characterisation
summary: Task planning, the problem of sequencing actions to reach a goal from an initial state, is a core capability requirement for autonomous robotic systems. Whether large language models (LLMs) can serve as viable planners alongside classical symbolic methods remains an open question. We present PyPDDLEngine, an open-source Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) simulation engine that exposes planning operations as LLM tool calls through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Rather than committing to a complete action sequence upfront, the LLM acts as an interactive search policy that selects one action at a time, observes each resulting state, and can reset and retry. We evaluate four approaches on 102 International Planning Competition (IPC) Blocksworld instances under a uniform 180-second budget: Fast Downward lama-first and seq-sat-lama-2011 as classical baselines, direct LLM planning (Claude Haiku 4.5), and agentic LLM planning via PyPDDLEngine. Fast Downward achieves 85.3% success. The direct and agentic LLM approaches achieve 63.7% and 66.7%, respectively, a consistent but modest three-percentage-point advantage for the agentic approach at $5.7\times$ higher token cost per solution. Across most co-solved difficulty blocks, both LLM approaches produce shorter plans than seq-sat-lama-2011 despite its iterative quality improvement, a result consistent with training-data recall rather than generalisable planning. These results suggest that agentic gains depend on the nature of environmental feedback. Coding agents benefit from externally grounded signals such as compiler errors and test failures, whereas PDDL step feedback is self-assessed, leaving the agent to evaluate its own progress without external verification.

AI.tldr: LLM-based agentic planning with PDDL simulation shows modest 3% improvement over direct LLM planning but at 5.7× higher token cost, achieving 66.7% success vs 85.3% for classical planners on Blocksworld tasks.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs can serve as viable planners alongside classical symbolic methods by testing them in interactive planning environments with state feedback, rather than committing to complete action sequences upfront.
AI.method: Developed PyPDDLEngine, an open-source PDDL simulation engine that exposes planning operations as LLM tool calls through MCP interface. LLM acts as interactive search policy selecting one action at a time, observing resulting states, and can reset/retry. Compared four approaches on 102 IPC Blocksworld instances: Fast Downward lama-first, seq-sat-lama-2011, direct LLM planning (Claude Haiku 4.5), and agentic LLM planning via PyPDDLEngine.
AI.result: Fast Downward achieved 85.3% success. Direct LLM planning achieved 63.7%, agentic LLM planning achieved 66.7% (3% advantage). Agentic approach had 5.7× higher token cost per solution. Both LLM approaches produced shorter plans than seq-sat-lama-2011 across most co-solved difficulty blocks.
AI.conclusion: Agentic gains depend on environmental feedback nature: coding agents benefit from externally grounded signals (compiler errors, test failures), while PDDL step feedback is self-assessed, leaving agents to evaluate their own progress without external verification. LLM planning performance likely reflects training-data recall rather than generalizable planning capabilities.

title: Cultural Perspectives and Expectations for Generative AI: A Global Survey Approach
summary: There is a lack of empirical evidence about global attitudes around whether and how GenAI should represent cultures. This paper assesses understandings and beliefs about culture as it relates to GenAI from a large-scale global survey. We gathered data about what culture means to different groups, and about how GenAI should approach the representation of cultural artifacts, concepts, or values. We distill working definitions of culture directly from these communities to build an understanding of its conceptual complexities and how they relate to representations in Generative AI. We survey from across parts of Europe, North and South America, Asia, and Africa. We conclude with a set of recommendations for Culture and GenAI development. These include participatory approaches, prioritizing specific cultural dimensions beyond geography, such as religion and tradition, and a sensitivity framework for addressing cultural ``redlines''.

AI.tldr: Global survey reveals diverse cultural perspectives on GenAI representation, leading to participatory recommendations for culturally sensitive AI development.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of empirical evidence about global attitudes regarding whether and how Generative AI should represent cultures, necessitating a comprehensive study to understand diverse cultural perspectives and inform responsible AI development.
AI.method: Conducted a large-scale global survey across Europe, North and South America, Asia, and Africa to gather data on cultural definitions and GenAI representation preferences. Distilled working definitions of culture directly from communities to understand conceptual complexities and their relation to AI representations.
AI.result: Survey revealed diverse understandings of culture across global communities and identified specific preferences for how GenAI should approach representing cultural artifacts, concepts, and values. The research generated working definitions of culture based on community perspectives.
AI.conclusion: Proposes recommendations for Culture and GenAI development including: participatory approaches, prioritizing specific cultural dimensions beyond geography (such as religion and tradition), and implementing a sensitivity framework for addressing cultural "redlines" to ensure responsible and culturally sensitive AI representation.

title: Aggregative Semantics for Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks
summary: Formal argumentation is being used increasingly in artificial intelligence as an effective and understandable way to model potentially conflicting pieces of information, called arguments, and identify so-called acceptable arguments depending on a chosen semantics. This paper deals with the specific context of Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks (QBAF), where arguments have intrinsic weights and can attack or support each other. In this context, we introduce a novel family of gradual semantics, called aggregative semantics. In order to deal with situations in which attackers and supporters do not play a symmetric role, and in contrast to modular semantics, we propose to aggregate attackers and supporters separately. This leads to a three-stage computation, which consists in computing a global weight for attackers and another for supporters, before aggregating these two values with the intrinsic weight of the argument. We discuss the properties that the three aggregation functions should satisfy depending on the context, as well as their relationships with the classical principles for gradual semantics. This discussion is supported by various simple examples, as well as a final example on which five hundred aggregative semantics are tested and compared, illustrating the range of possible behaviours with aggregative semantics. Decomposing the computation into three distinct and interpretable steps leads to a more parametrisable computation: it keeps the bipolarity one step further than what is done in the literature, and it leads to more understandable gradual semantics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces aggregative semantics for Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks, a novel three-stage approach that separately aggregates attackers and supporters before combining them with intrinsic argument weights, offering more parametrisable and interpretable gradual semantics.
AI.motivation: Existing gradual semantics in Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks often treat attackers and supporters symmetrically, which may not reflect real-world scenarios where they play different roles. There's a need for more flexible, interpretable semantics that can handle asymmetric relationships between attackers and supporters while maintaining bipolarity.
AI.method: Proposes aggregative semantics with three-stage computation: 1) compute global weight for attackers, 2) compute global weight for supporters, 3) aggregate these two values with the intrinsic weight of the argument. This approach separates the aggregation of attackers and supporters, unlike modular semantics, allowing for asymmetric treatment.
AI.result: The paper establishes properties that aggregation functions should satisfy in different contexts and relates them to classical principles for gradual semantics. Through examples and testing 500 aggregative semantics on a final example, the approach demonstrates a wide range of possible behaviors while maintaining interpretability and parametrisability.
AI.conclusion: Aggregative semantics provide a more flexible, interpretable approach to gradual semantics in QBAFs by decomposing computation into three distinct steps, preserving bipolarity at a deeper level than existing methods, and offering greater parametrisability while maintaining understandability.

title: Structured Multidimensional Representation Learning for Large Language Models
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures. Preprint of a journal submission
summary: Transformer architectures achieve state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of pattern recognition and natural language processing tasks, but their scaling is accompanied by substantial parameter growth and redundancy in the embedding dimension. In this work, we introduce a structured spectral factorization of the embedding space based on the L-product for third-order tensors. By reshaping token representations into spectral tensor slices and performing attention and feed-forward operations in the transform domain, we obtain a Tensor Transformer architecture that decomposes the encoder into p independent spectral sub-transformers while preserving standard Transformer semantics. We prove that the proposed L-Transformer is spectrally equivalent to p parallel Transformers operating on reduceddimensional embeddings, which yields approximately 1/p reduction (up to lower-order terms such as biases and normalization parameters) in encoder parameters under fixed total embedding size. When instantiated with a real-valued Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), the method remains fully differentiable and compatible with existing training pipelines. Beyond compression, the spectral decomposition introduces an inductive bias over embedding frequencies, enabling slice-dependent frequency scaling that improves generalization. Experiments on IMDB and AG~News show that the proposed model can substantially reduce encoder parameters (up to 75\% for p=4) while maintaining competitive accuracy. On IMDB, the tensorized encoder matches or improves upon the standard baseline under compression, whereas on AG~News at moderate width we observe a small accuracy decrease in exchange for a 4 times encoder reduction; at BERT-base width (d=768), performance returns to parity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Tensor Transformer architecture that uses structured spectral factorization via the L-product to decompose embeddings into spectral tensor slices, achieving significant parameter reduction while maintaining Transformer semantics and competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Transformer architectures suffer from substantial parameter growth and redundancy in embedding dimensions as they scale. The authors aim to address this by developing a more efficient representation that reduces parameters while preserving model capacity and introducing beneficial inductive biases.
AI.method: The method introduces a structured spectral factorization of embedding space using the L-product for third-order tensors. Token representations are reshaped into spectral tensor slices, and attention/feed-forward operations are performed in the transform domain. This creates a Tensor Transformer architecture that decomposes the encoder into p independent spectral sub-transformers while preserving standard Transformer semantics. The approach uses real-valued Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to remain fully differentiable and compatible with existing training pipelines.
AI.result: The L-Transformer achieves approximately 1/p reduction in encoder parameters (up to 75% for p=4) while maintaining competitive accuracy. On IMDB, the tensorized encoder matches or improves upon standard baselines under compression. On AG~News, moderate width shows small accuracy decrease for 4× encoder reduction, but at BERT-base width (d=768), performance returns to parity with standard Transformers.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Tensor Transformer architecture successfully reduces parameter redundancy through spectral factorization while preserving Transformer semantics. Beyond compression benefits, the spectral decomposition introduces frequency-based inductive biases that can improve generalization. The method offers a practical approach to scaling Transformers more efficiently without sacrificing performance.

title: Offline Materials Optimization with CliqueFlowmer
summary: Recent advances in deep learning inspired neural network-based approaches to computational materials discovery (CMD). A plethora of problems in this field involve finding materials that optimize a target property. Nevertheless, the increasingly popular generative modeling methods are ineffective at boldly exploring attractive regions of the materials space due to their maximum likelihood training. In this work, we offer an alternative CMD technique based on offline model-based optimization (MBO) that fuses direct optimization of a target material property into generation. To that end, we introduce a domain-specific model, dubbed CliqueFlowmer, that incorporates recent advances of clique-based MBO into transformer and flow generation. We validate CliqueFlowmer's optimization abilities and show that materials it produces strongly outperform those provided by generative baselines. To enable employment of CliqueFlowmer in specialized materials optimization problems and support interdisciplinary research, we open-source our code at https://github.com/znowu/CliqueFlowmer.

AI.tldr: CliqueFlowmer is a novel computational materials discovery method combining clique-based model-based optimization with transformer and flow generation to directly optimize target material properties, outperforming traditional generative approaches.
AI.motivation: Current generative modeling methods for computational materials discovery are ineffective at exploring attractive regions of materials space due to maximum likelihood training limitations, creating a need for alternative approaches that directly optimize target properties.
AI.method: CliqueFlowmer integrates clique-based model-based optimization (MBO) with transformer and flow generation architectures, enabling direct optimization of target material properties during generation rather than relying on maximum likelihood training.
AI.result: CliqueFlowmer demonstrates superior optimization capabilities compared to generative baselines, producing materials that strongly outperform those generated by traditional methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed offline model-based optimization approach with CliqueFlowmer offers an effective alternative to generative methods for computational materials discovery, with open-source code available to support specialized optimization problems and interdisciplinary research.

title: Let's Talk, Not Type: An Oral-First Multi-Agent Architecture for Guaraní
summary: Although artificial intelligence (AI) and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) systems are often presented as universal solutions, their design remains predominantly text-first, underserving primarily oral languages and indigenous communities. This position paper uses Guaraní, an official and widely spoken language of Paraguay, as a case study to argue that language support in AI remains insufficient unless it aligns with lived oral practices. We propose an alternative to the standard "text-to-speech" pipeline, proposing instead an oral-first multi-agent architecture. By decoupling Guaraní natural language understanding from dedicated agents for conversation state and community-led governance, we demonstrate a technical framework that respects indigenous data sovereignty and diglossia. Our work moves beyond mere recognition to focus on turn-taking, repair, and shared context as the primary locus of interaction. We conclude that for AI to be truly culturally grounded, it must shift from adapting oral languages to text-centric systems to treating spoken conversation as a first-class design requirement, ensuring digital ecosystems empower rather than overlook diverse linguistic practices.

AI.tldr: This position paper critiques text-first AI/HCI design for underserving oral languages, using Guaraní as a case study to propose an oral-first multi-agent architecture that respects indigenous data sovereignty and treats spoken conversation as a first-class design requirement.
AI.motivation: Current AI and HCI systems are predominantly text-first and universalist, which underserves primarily oral languages and indigenous communities. The paper argues that language support in AI remains insufficient unless it aligns with lived oral practices, using Guaraní (an official language of Paraguay) as a case study to highlight this gap.
AI.method: The paper proposes an alternative to standard "text-to-speech" pipelines: an oral-first multi-agent architecture that decouples Guaraní natural language understanding from dedicated agents for conversation state and community-led governance. This technical framework focuses on turn-taking, repair, and shared context as primary interaction loci rather than mere recognition.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates a technical framework that respects indigenous data sovereignty and diglossia (the coexistence of multiple language varieties). It moves beyond simple language recognition to address the fundamental aspects of oral conversation that are essential for culturally grounded AI systems.
AI.conclusion: For AI to be truly culturally grounded, it must shift from adapting oral languages to text-centric systems to treating spoken conversation as a first-class design requirement. This ensures digital ecosystems empower rather than overlook diverse linguistic practices, with indigenous data sovereignty and community-led governance as essential components.

title: CodeScout: Contextual Problem Statement Enhancement for Software Agents
summary: Current AI-powered code assistance tools often struggle with poorly-defined problem statements that lack sufficient task context and requirements specification. Recent analysis of software engineering agents reveals that failures on such underspecified requests are highly correlated with longer trajectories involving either over-exploration or repeated attempts at applying the same fix without proper evolution or testing, leading to suboptimal outcomes across software development tasks. We introduce CodeScout, a contextual query refinement approach that systematically converts underspecified user requests into comprehensive, actionable problem statements through lightweight pre-exploration of the target codebase.
