In the first stage, the model performs deliberate spatial pre-thinking to infer viewpoint relations and spatial transformations across views, forming an intermediate workspace that goes beyond a simple re-description. In the second stage, the model conducts question-driven reasoning conditioned on this workspace to produce the final prediction. We train ViewFusion with synthetic reasoning supervision followed by reinforcement learning using GRPO, which improves answer correctness while stabilizing the intended two-stage generation behavior. On MMSI-Bench, ViewFusion improves accuracy by 5.3\% over Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, with the largest gains on examples that require genuine cross-view alignment.

AI.tldr: ViewFusion is a two-stage framework for multi-view spatial reasoning that separates cross-view spatial pre-alignment from question answering, improving performance on viewpoint transformation and occlusion-sensitive cases.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models underutilize cross-view relations in multi-view spatial reasoning, relying instead on single-image shortcuts that lead to fragile performance on viewpoint transformation and occlusion-sensitive cases.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: 1) Spatial pre-alignment stage performs deliberate spatial pre-thinking to infer viewpoint relations and transformations across views, creating an intermediate workspace; 2) Question-driven reasoning stage produces final predictions conditioned on this workspace. Trained with synthetic reasoning supervision followed by reinforcement learning using GRPO.
AI.result: On MMSI-Bench, ViewFusion improves accuracy by 5.3% over Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, with largest gains on examples requiring genuine cross-view alignment.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly separating cross-view spatial pre-alignment from question answering enables more robust multi-view spatial reasoning, addressing limitations of current models that rely on single-image shortcuts.

title: FlashPrefill: Instantaneous Pattern Discovery and Thresholding for Ultra-Fast Long-Context Prefilling
summary: Long-context modeling is a pivotal capability for Large Language Models, yet the quadratic complexity of attention remains a critical bottleneck, particularly during the compute-intensive prefilling phase. While various sparse attention mechanisms have been explored, they typically suffer from either significant search latency or insufficient sparsity. In this paper, we propose FlashPrefill, a framework enabling ultra-fast prefilling via instantaneous pattern discovery and thresholding. FlashPrefill leverages a fast block-searching technique to simultaneously locate dynamic vertical, slash, and block-sparse attention patterns. Crucially, it introduces a dynamic thresholding mechanism that bypasses the prohibitive overhead of sorting or accumulating attention scores while effectively eliminating the long-tail distribution to enhance sparsity. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FlashPrefill achieves a substantial leap in efficiency, delivering an unprecedented 27.78x speedup on 256K sequences. Notably, unlike existing methods that incur efficiency degradation on shorter contexts, FlashPrefill maintains a 1.71x speedup even at a 4K context length, demonstrating its robustness and practical utility across varying sequence scales.

AI.tldr: FlashPrefill is a framework for ultra-fast prefilling in long-context LLMs using instantaneous pattern discovery and dynamic thresholding to achieve up to 27.78x speedup on 256K sequences.
AI.motivation: The quadratic complexity of attention in LLMs creates a critical bottleneck during compute-intensive prefilling, especially for long contexts. Existing sparse attention methods suffer from either significant search latency or insufficient sparsity.
AI.method: FlashPrefill uses fast block-searching to locate dynamic vertical, slash, and block-sparse attention patterns simultaneously. It introduces a dynamic thresholding mechanism that avoids sorting or accumulating attention scores while eliminating long-tail distributions to enhance sparsity.
AI.result: Achieves 27.78x speedup on 256K sequences and maintains 1.71x speedup even at 4K context length, demonstrating robustness across varying sequence scales without efficiency degradation on shorter contexts.
AI.conclusion: FlashPrefill provides a practical solution for efficient long-context modeling by overcoming the quadratic attention bottleneck through instantaneous pattern discovery and intelligent thresholding, maintaining performance across different context lengths.

title: Abductive Reasoning with Syllogistic Forms in Large Language Models
comment: Published in Proceedings of the 3rd International Conference on Human and Artificial Rationalities (HAR 2024), LNCS 15504, pp. 3-17
summary: Research in AI using Large-Language Models (LLMs) is rapidly evolving, and the comparison of their performance with human reasoning has become a key concern. Prior studies have indicated that LLMs and humans share similar biases, such as dismissing logically valid inferences that contradict common beliefs. However, criticizing LLMs for these biases might be unfair, considering our reasoning not only involves formal deduction but also abduction, which draws tentative conclusions from limited information. Abduction can be regarded as the inverse form of syllogism in its basic structure, that is, a process of drawing a minor premise from a major premise and conclusion. This paper explores the accuracy of LLMs in abductive reasoning by converting a syllogistic dataset into one suitable for abduction. It aims to investigate whether the state-of-the-art LLMs exhibit biases in abduction and to identify potential areas for improvement, emphasizing the importance of contextualized reasoning beyond formal deduction. This investigation is vital for advancing the understanding and application of LLMs in complex reasoning tasks, offering insights into bridging the gap between machine and human cognition.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether state-of-the-art LLMs exhibit biases in abductive reasoning by converting syllogistic datasets to test abduction, aiming to understand if criticizing LLMs for shared human biases is fair given that human reasoning involves both formal deduction and abduction.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address whether it's fair to criticize LLMs for sharing human biases in reasoning, since human reasoning involves not just formal deduction but also abduction (drawing tentative conclusions from limited information). Prior studies show LLMs and humans share similar biases like dismissing logically valid inferences that contradict common beliefs, but this criticism may overlook the role of abduction in human cognition.
AI.method: The method involves converting a syllogistic dataset into one suitable for testing abductive reasoning. Abduction is treated as the inverse form of syllogism - drawing a minor premise from a major premise and conclusion. The paper tests state-of-the-art LLMs on this converted dataset to evaluate their accuracy and biases in abductive reasoning.
AI.result: The abstract doesn't specify concrete results, but indicates the investigation aims to determine whether LLMs exhibit biases in abduction and identify potential areas for improvement. The focus is on understanding LLM performance in contextualized reasoning beyond formal deduction.
AI.conclusion: The investigation is vital for advancing understanding of LLMs in complex reasoning tasks and bridging the gap between machine and human cognition. The paper emphasizes the importance of evaluating LLMs on contextualized reasoning that includes abduction, not just formal deduction, to provide fairer assessments of their reasoning capabilities.

title: PONTE: Personalized Orchestration for Natural Language Trustworthy Explanations
summary: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) seeks to enhance the transparency and accountability of machine learning systems, yet most methods follow a one-size-fits-all paradigm that neglects user differences in expertise, goals, and cognitive needs. Although Large Language Models can translate technical explanations into natural language, they introduce challenges related to faithfulness and hallucinations. To address these challenges, we present PONTE (Personalized Orchestration for Natural language Trustworthy Explanations), a human-in-the-loop framework for adaptive and reliable XAI narratives. PONTE models personalization as a closed-loop validation and adaptation process rather than prompt engineering. It combines: (i) a low-dimensional preference model capturing stylistic requirements; (ii) a preference-conditioned generator grounded in structured XAI artifacts; and (iii) verification modules enforcing numerical faithfulness, informational completeness, and stylistic alignment, optionally supported by retrieval-grounded argumentation. User feedback iteratively updates the preference state, enabling quick personalization. Automatic and human evaluations across healthcare and finance domains show that the verification-refinement loop substantially improves completeness and stylistic alignment over validation-free generation. Human studies further confirm strong agreement between intended preference vectors and perceived style, robustness to generation stochasticity, and consistently positive quality assessments.

AI.tldr: PONTE is a human-in-the-loop framework for personalized, trustworthy XAI explanations that uses closed-loop validation and adaptation to address LLM hallucination issues while tailoring explanations to individual user preferences.
AI.motivation: Current XAI methods use a one-size-fits-all approach that ignores user differences in expertise, goals, and cognitive needs. While LLMs can translate technical explanations into natural language, they suffer from faithfulness issues and hallucinations, creating a need for personalized, reliable XAI narratives.
AI.method: PONTE models personalization as a closed-loop validation and adaptation process with three components: (1) low-dimensional preference model capturing stylistic requirements, (2) preference-conditioned generator grounded in structured XAI artifacts, and (3) verification modules enforcing numerical faithfulness, informational completeness, and stylistic alignment. User feedback iteratively updates preference states, enabling quick personalization.
AI.result: Automatic and human evaluations in healthcare and finance domains show the verification-refinement loop substantially improves completeness and stylistic alignment over validation-free generation. Human studies confirm strong agreement between intended preference vectors and perceived style, robustness to generation stochasticity, and consistently positive quality assessments.
AI.conclusion: PONTE provides an effective framework for personalized, trustworthy XAI explanations by combining preference modeling, grounded generation, and verification modules in a closed-loop adaptation process that addresses LLM hallucination issues while tailoring explanations to individual user needs.

title: Wisdom of the AI Crowd (AI-CROWD) for Ground Truth Approximation in Content Analysis: A Research Protocol & Validation Using Eleven Large Language Models
summary: Large-scale content analysis is increasingly limited by the absence of observable ground truth or gold-standard labels, as creating such benchmarks through extensive human coding becomes impractical for massive datasets due to high time, cost, and consistency challenges. To overcome this barrier, we introduce the AI-CROWD protocol, which approximates ground truth by leveraging the collective outputs of an ensemble of large language models (LLMs). Rather than asserting that the resulting labels are true ground truth, the protocol generates a consensus-based approximation derived from convergent and divergent inferences across multiple models. By aggregating outputs via majority voting and interrogating agreement/disagreement patterns with diagnostic metrics, AI-CROWD identifies high-confidence classifications while flagging potential ambiguity or model-specific biases.

AI.tldr: AI-CROWD protocol uses ensemble of LLMs to approximate ground truth labels for large-scale content analysis when human coding is impractical.
AI.motivation: Large-scale content analysis is limited by absence of observable ground truth due to impracticality of extensive human coding (high time, cost, consistency challenges). Need alternative approach for massive datasets.
AI.method: AI-CROWD protocol leverages collective outputs of ensemble of large language models (LLMs) to approximate ground truth. Uses majority voting to aggregate outputs and diagnostic metrics to analyze agreement/disagreement patterns, identifying high-confidence classifications while flagging ambiguity or model-specific biases.
AI.result: Protocol generates consensus-based approximation derived from convergent and divergent inferences across multiple models, rather than asserting true ground truth. Enables identification of high-confidence classifications with awareness of potential ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: AI-CROWD provides practical solution for large-scale content analysis by approximating ground truth through LLM ensemble consensus, overcoming limitations of human coding for massive datasets while acknowledging approximation nature of results.

title: LIT-RAGBench: Benchmarking Generator Capabilities of Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: Published as a conference paper at LREC 2026
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a framework in which a Generator, such as a Large Language Model (LLM), produces answers by retrieving documents from an external collection using a Retriever. In practice, Generators must integrate evidence from long contexts, perform multi-step reasoning, interpret tables, and abstain when evidence is missing. However, existing benchmarks for Generators provide limited coverage, with none enabling simultaneous evaluation of multiple capabilities under unified conditions. To bridge the gap between existing evaluations and practical use, we introduce LIT-RAGBench (the Logic, Integration, Table, Reasoning, and Abstention RAG Generator Benchmark), which defines five categories: Integration, Reasoning, Logic, Table, and Abstention, each further divided into practical evaluation aspects. LIT-RAGBench systematically covers patterns combining multiple aspects across categories. By using fictional entities and scenarios, LIT-RAGBench evaluates answers grounded in the provided external documents. The dataset consists of 114 human-constructed Japanese questions and an English version generated by machine translation with human curation. We use LLM-as-a-Judge for scoring and report category-wise and overall accuracy. Across API-based and open-weight models, no model exceeds 90% overall accuracy. By making strengths and weaknesses measurable within each category, LIT-RAGBench serves as a valuable metric for model selection in practical RAG deployments and for building RAG-specialized models. We release LIT-RAGBench, including the dataset and evaluation code, at https://github.com/Koki-Itai/LIT-RAGBench.

AI.tldr: LIT-RAGBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating RAG generators across five key capabilities: Integration, Reasoning, Logic, Table interpretation, and Abstention, using fictional scenarios to ensure grounding in provided documents.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG benchmarks provide limited coverage and don't enable simultaneous evaluation of multiple practical capabilities under unified conditions, creating a gap between evaluation and real-world RAG deployment needs.
AI.method: Created a benchmark with 114 human-constructed Japanese questions (plus English translation) covering five categories: Integration, Reasoning, Logic, Table, and Abstention. Uses fictional entities/scenarios to ensure answers are grounded in provided documents, and employs LLM-as-a-Judge for scoring.
AI.result: No model (API-based or open-weight) exceeded 90% overall accuracy. The benchmark reveals measurable strengths and weaknesses across categories, providing actionable insights for model selection and development.
AI.conclusion: LIT-RAGBench serves as a valuable metric for practical RAG deployment model selection and for building RAG-specialized models, bridging the gap between existing evaluations and real-world requirements.

title: SPOT: Span-level Pause-of-Thought for Efficient and Interpretable Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Explicit Chain-of-Thought improves the reasoning performance of large language models but often incurs high inference cost due to verbose token-level traces. While recent approaches reduce this overhead via concise prompting or step pruning, they largely truncate what the model says rather than internalize what the model thinks. Latent reasoning offers a promising alternative by performing computation in the hidden space, yet prior methods face two critical challenges. Many existing approaches rely on rigid point-to-point alignment, forcing a latent token to approximate the final representation of a reasoning step, which can be insufficient to capture the dense, variable-length semantics of an entire reasoning segment. Furthermore, these methods often suffer from a lack of interpretability: latent states are commonly produced by unconstrained optimization or embedding mixing, yielding vectors that are difficult to decode or audit under the pretrained language head. We propose SPOT, a flexible framework that compresses explicit CoT into compact latent pause tokens without enforcing a fixed response template. At the core of SPOT is Span-level Semantic Alignment, a Sinkhorn optimal-transport objective that softly matches each pause token to the semantics of an entire reasoning segment, overcoming the rigidity of step-end alignment. To further improve interpretability, SPOT introduces a Frozen-Head Decoding Constraint that keeps latent states directly decodable as token distributions under the frozen pretrained LM head, enabling readable keyword interpretations of latent thoughts. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SPOT improves accuracy by 2.3 points on average while reducing generated tokens by 37.5% and provides faithful semantic interpretations of the latent reasoning process.

AI.tldr: SPOT is a framework that compresses explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning into compact latent pause tokens using span-level semantic alignment and frozen-head decoding, improving accuracy while reducing token generation by 37.5%.
AI.motivation: Explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning improves LLM performance but incurs high inference costs due to verbose token traces. Existing approaches either truncate model outputs or use latent reasoning with rigid alignment and poor interpretability, failing to capture dense, variable-length reasoning semantics while producing uninterpretable latent states.
AI.method: SPOT uses Span-level Semantic Alignment with a Sinkhorn optimal-transport objective to softly match each pause token to entire reasoning segments, overcoming rigid step-end alignment. It also employs a Frozen-Head Decoding Constraint to keep latent states directly decodable as token distributions under the frozen pretrained LM head for interpretability.
AI.result: SPOT improves accuracy by 2.3 points on average across reasoning benchmarks while reducing generated tokens by 37.5%. The framework provides faithful semantic interpretations of the latent reasoning process through decodable latent states.
AI.conclusion: SPOT successfully addresses the dual challenges of rigid alignment and poor interpretability in latent reasoning by introducing flexible span-level semantic alignment and frozen-head decoding constraints, enabling efficient and interpretable compression of explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning.

title: Mind the Gap: Pitfalls of LLM Alignment with Asian Public Opinion
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in multilingual, multicultural settings, yet their reliance on predominantly English-centric training data risks misalignment with the diverse cultural values of different societies. In this paper, we present a comprehensive, multilingual audit of the cultural alignment of contemporary LLMs including GPT-4o-Mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Llama 3.2, Mistral and Gemma 3 across India, East Asia and Southeast Asia. Our study specifically focuses on the sensitive domain of religion as the prism for broader alignment. To facilitate this, we conduct a multi-faceted analysis of every LLM's internal representations, using log-probs/logits, to compare the model's opinion distributions against ground-truth public attitudes. We find that while the popular models generally align with public opinion on broad social issues, they consistently fail to accurately represent religious viewpoints, especially those of minority groups, often amplifying negative stereotypes. Lightweight interventions, such as demographic priming and native language prompting, partially mitigate but do not eliminate these cultural gaps. We further show that downstream evaluations on bias benchmarks (such as CrowS-Pairs, IndiBias, ThaiCLI, KoBBQ) reveal persistent harms and under-representation in sensitive contexts. Our findings underscore the urgent need for systematic, regionally grounded audits to ensure equitable global deployment of LLMs.

AI.tldr: LLMs show cultural misalignment with religious values in India, East Asia, and Southeast Asia, despite general alignment on social issues, with minority religious viewpoints particularly underrepresented and stereotyped.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in multilingual, multicultural settings but rely on English-centric training data, risking misalignment with diverse cultural values across different societies, particularly in sensitive domains like religion.
AI.method: Comprehensive multilingual audit of LLMs (GPT-4o-Mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Llama 3.2, Mistral, Gemma 3) across India, East Asia, and Southeast Asia using internal representation analysis (log-probs/logits) to compare model opinion distributions against ground-truth public attitudes, with interventions like demographic priming and native language prompting.
AI.result: Models generally align with public opinion on broad social issues but consistently fail to accurately represent religious viewpoints, especially minority groups, often amplifying negative stereotypes. Lightweight interventions partially mitigate but don't eliminate cultural gaps. Downstream bias benchmarks reveal persistent harms and under-representation in sensitive contexts.
AI.conclusion: Urgent need for systematic, regionally grounded audits to ensure equitable global deployment of LLMs, as current models show significant cultural misalignment in religious domains despite interventions.

title: The Art That Poses Back: Assessing AI Pastiches after Contemporary Artworks
summary: This study explores artificial visual creativity, focusing on ChatGPT's ability to generate new images intentionally pastiching original artworks such as paintings, drawings, sculptures and installations. The process involved twelve artists from Romania, Bulgaria, France, Austria, and the United Kingdom, each invited to contribute with three of their artworks and to grade and comment on the AI-generated versions. The analysis combines human evaluation with computational methods aimed at detecting visual and stylistic similarities or divergences between the original works and their AI-produced renditions. The results point to a significant gap between color and texture-based similarity and compositional, conceptual, and perceptual one. Consequently, we advocate for the use of a "style transfer dashboard" of complementary metrics to evaluate the similarity between pastiches and originals, rather than using a single style metric. The artists' comments revealed limitations of ChatGPT's pastiches after contemporary artworks, which were perceived by the authors of the originals as lacking dimensionality, context, and intentional sense, and seeming more of a paraphrase or an approximate quotation rather than as a valuable, emotion-evoking artwork.

AI.tldr: ChatGPT's ability to generate pastiches of original artworks was evaluated by artists and computational methods, revealing significant gaps between color/texture similarity and compositional/conceptual similarity, leading to recommendations for multi-metric evaluation dashboards.
AI.motivation: To explore artificial visual creativity by assessing ChatGPT's capability to intentionally generate pastiches of original artworks and understand the gap between computational similarity metrics and human artistic evaluation.
AI.method: Involved 12 international artists contributing 3 artworks each; combined human evaluation (artist grading/comments) with computational methods detecting visual/stylistic similarities between originals and AI-generated pastiches.
AI.result: Significant gap between color/texture-based similarity and compositional/conceptual/perceptual similarity; artists perceived ChatGPT pastiches as lacking dimensionality, context, intentional sense, and emotional value, appearing more as paraphrases than valuable artworks.
AI.conclusion: Advocates for using a "style transfer dashboard" of complementary metrics rather than single style metrics to evaluate similarity between pastiches and originals, acknowledging current limitations in AI's ability to create meaningful artistic pastiches.

title: Transparent AI for Mathematics: Transformer-Based Large Language Models for Mathematical Entity Relationship Extraction with XAI
summary: Mathematical text understanding is a challenging task due to the presence of specialized entities and complex relationships between them. This study formulates mathematical problem interpretation as a Mathematical Entity Relation Extraction (MERE) task, where operands are treated as entities and operators as their relationships. Transformer-based models are applied to automatically extract these relations from mathematical text, with Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) achieving the best performance, reaching an accuracy of 99.39%. To enhance transparency and trust in the model's predictions, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is incorporated using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP). The explainability analysis reveals how specific textual and mathematical features influence relation prediction, providing insights into feature importance and model behavior. By combining transformer-based learning, a task-specific dataset, and explainable modeling, this work offers an effective and interpretable framework for MERE, supporting future applications in automated problem solving, knowledge graph construction, and intelligent educational systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a transformer-based approach for Mathematical Entity Relation Extraction (MERE) that treats mathematical operands as entities and operators as relationships, achieving 99.39% accuracy with BERT and incorporating SHAP for explainability.
AI.motivation: Mathematical text understanding is challenging due to specialized entities and complex relationships. There's a need for automated extraction of mathematical relations to support applications like automated problem solving, knowledge graph construction, and intelligent educational systems.
AI.method: Formulates mathematical problem interpretation as MERE task where operands are entities and operators are relationships. Uses transformer-based models (including BERT) for relation extraction and incorporates SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) for explainable AI to enhance transparency.
AI.result: BERT achieved the best performance with 99.39% accuracy in mathematical relation extraction. SHAP analysis provided insights into how specific textual and mathematical features influence relation predictions, revealing feature importance and model behavior.
AI.conclusion: The work offers an effective and interpretable framework for MERE by combining transformer-based learning, task-specific datasets, and explainable modeling. This supports future applications in automated problem solving, knowledge graph construction, and intelligent educational systems.

title: Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in Large Language Models: The Case of Wason's Selection Task
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of EACL 2026
summary: As large language models (LLMs) advance in linguistic competence, their reasoning abilities are gaining increasing attention. In humans, reasoning often performs well in domain specific settings, particularly in normative rather than purely formal contexts. Although prior studies have compared LLM and human reasoning, the domain specificity of LLM reasoning remains underexplored. In this study, we introduce a new Wason Selection Task dataset that explicitly encodes deontic modality to systematically distinguish deontic from descriptive conditionals, and use it to examine LLMs' conditional reasoning under deontic rules. We further analyze whether observed error patterns are better explained by confirmation bias (a tendency to seek rule-supporting evidence) or by matching bias (a tendency to ignore negation and select items that lexically match elements of the rule). Results show that, like humans, LLMs reason better with deontic rules and display matching-bias-like errors. Together, these findings suggest that the performance of LLMs varies systematically across rule types and that their error patterns can parallel well-known human biases in this paradigm.

AI.tldr: LLMs show human-like domain-specific reasoning patterns: better performance with deontic (normative) rules than descriptive ones, and exhibit matching bias errors similar to humans in Wason Selection Tasks.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs exhibit domain-specific reasoning patterns similar to humans, particularly examining if their reasoning performance varies between deontic (normative) and descriptive conditionals, and to analyze whether their error patterns align with known human cognitive biases like confirmation bias or matching bias.
AI.method: Created a new Wason Selection Task dataset that explicitly encodes deontic modality to distinguish deontic from descriptive conditionals. Used this dataset to systematically examine LLMs' conditional reasoning under deontic rules. Analyzed error patterns to determine whether they align more with confirmation bias (seeking rule-supporting evidence) or matching bias (ignoring negation and selecting lexically matching items).
AI.result: LLMs, like humans, reason better with deontic rules than with descriptive conditionals. Their error patterns show matching-bias-like errors (tendency to ignore negation and select items that lexically match rule elements) rather than confirmation bias. Performance varies systematically across rule types, with deontic rules eliciting more accurate reasoning.
AI.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic variation in reasoning performance across different rule types, mirroring human domain-specific reasoning patterns. Their error patterns parallel well-known human cognitive biases, particularly matching bias, suggesting that LLM reasoning can reflect similar cognitive constraints and heuristics as human reasoning in this paradigm.

title: From Prompting to Preference Optimization: A Comparative Study of LLM-based Automated Essay Scoring
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently reshaped Automated Essay Scoring (AES), yet prior studies typically examine individual techniques in isolation, limiting understanding of their relative merits for English as a Second Language (L2) writing. To bridge this gap, we presents a comprehensive comparison of major LLM-based AES paradigms on IELTS Writing Task~2. On this unified benchmark, we evaluate four approaches: (i) encoder-based classification fine-tuning, (ii) zero- and few-shot prompting, (iii) instruction tuning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and (iv) Supervised Fine-Tuning combined with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and RAG. Our results reveal clear accuracy-cost-robustness trade-offs across methods, the best configuration, integrating k-SFT and RAG, achieves the strongest overall results with F1-Score 93%. This study offers the first unified empirical comparison of modern LLM-based AES strategies for English L2, promising potential in auto-grading writing tasks. Code is public at https://github.com/MinhNguyenDS/LLM_AES-EnL2

AI.tldr: Comprehensive comparison of LLM-based AES paradigms for English L2 writing assessment on IELTS Task 2, revealing accuracy-cost-robustness trade-offs with best configuration achieving 93% F1-Score.
AI.motivation: Prior studies examine individual LLM-based AES techniques in isolation, limiting understanding of their relative merits for English as a Second Language (L2) writing assessment.
AI.method: Unified benchmark evaluation of four LLM-based AES approaches on IELTS Writing Task 2: (1) encoder-based classification fine-tuning, (2) zero- and few-shot prompting, (3) instruction tuning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and (4) Supervised Fine-Tuning combined with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and RAG.
AI.result: Clear accuracy-cost-robustness trade-offs across methods; best configuration integrating k-SFT and RAG achieves strongest overall results with 93% F1-Score.
AI.conclusion: First unified empirical comparison of modern LLM-based AES strategies for English L2 writing, demonstrating promising potential for auto-grading writing tasks with identified optimal configurations.

title: Beyond Rows to Reasoning: Agentic Retrieval for Multimodal Spreadsheet Understanding and Editing
summary: Recent advances in multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to analyze enterprise spreadsheet workbooks containing millions of cells, cross-sheet dependencies, and embedded visual artifacts. However, state-of-the-art approaches exclude critical context through single-pass retrieval, lose data resolution through compression, and exceed LLM context windows through naive full-context injection, preventing reliable multi-step reasoning over complex enterprise workbooks. We introduce Beyond Rows to Reasoning (BRTR), a multimodal agentic framework for spreadsheet understanding that replaces single-pass retrieval with an iterative tool-calling loop, supporting end-to-end Excel workflows from complex analysis to structured editing. Supported by over 200 hours of expert human evaluation, BRTR achieves state-of-the-art performance across three frontier spreadsheet understanding benchmarks, surpassing prior methods by 25 percentage points on FRTR-Bench, 7 points on SpreadsheetLLM, and 32 points on FINCH. We evaluate five multimodal embedding models, identifying NVIDIA NeMo Retriever 1B as the top performer for mixed tabular and visual data, and vary nine LLMs. Ablation experiments confirm that the planner, retrieval, and iterative reasoning each contribute substantially, and cost analysis shows GPT-5.2 achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off. Throughout all evaluations, BRTR maintains full auditability through explicit tool-call traces.

AI.tldr: BRTR is a multimodal agentic framework for spreadsheet understanding that uses iterative tool-calling loops instead of single-pass retrieval, achieving SOTA performance on spreadsheet benchmarks while maintaining full auditability.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal RAG approaches for spreadsheet analysis have limitations: they exclude critical context through single-pass retrieval, lose data resolution through compression, and exceed LLM context windows through naive full-context injection, preventing reliable multi-step reasoning over complex enterprise workbooks.
AI.method: BRTR replaces single-pass retrieval with an iterative tool-calling loop that supports end-to-end Excel workflows. It uses multimodal embedding models (identifying NVIDIA NeMo Retriever 1B as top performer) and varies nine LLMs, with components including planner, retrieval, and iterative reasoning modules.
AI.result: BRTR achieves state-of-the-art performance across three spreadsheet benchmarks: surpassing prior methods by 25 percentage points on FRTR-Bench, 7 points on SpreadsheetLLM, and 32 points on FINCH. GPT-5.2 achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off. Ablation experiments confirm all components contribute substantially.
AI.conclusion: BRTR provides a robust framework for spreadsheet understanding that overcomes limitations of current approaches through iterative reasoning, maintains full auditability via explicit tool-call traces, and demonstrates superior performance on complex enterprise workbook analysis tasks.

title: Speak in Context: Multilingual ASR with Speech Context Alignment via Contrastive Learning
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has benefited from advances in pretrained speech and language models, yet most systems remain constrained to monolingual settings and short, isolated utterances. While recent efforts in context-aware ASR show promise, two key challenges persist: limited multilingual support and the absence of principled alignment between speech and contextual representations. In this paper, we introduce a context-aware multilingual ASR framework that supports diverse languages and accents while preserving the modularity of pretrained models. Our approach combines a frozen speech encoder and a decoder-only language model via a lightweight projection module, allowing structured context prompts, including dialogue history and biasing words, to guide transcription. To improve interaction between speech and context, we employ a contrastive learning objective that aligns their representations in a shared embedding space. Evaluations on over 1,500 hours of real-world conversational speech across 11 languages and 5 English dialects show that contextual input consistently improves recognition quality. Contrastive alignment provides additional gains when applied to different context types, with an overall performance gain of over 5%. These results highlight the importance of both contextual modeling and cross-modal alignment in multilingual ASR.

AI.tldr: A context-aware multilingual ASR framework that combines frozen speech encoder and decoder-only language model via lightweight projection, using contrastive learning to align speech and contextual representations, achieving over 5% performance gain across 11 languages and 5 English dialects.
AI.motivation: Most ASR systems remain constrained to monolingual settings and short, isolated utterances, with limited multilingual support and absence of principled alignment between speech and contextual representations. Recent context-aware ASR efforts lack comprehensive multilingual capabilities and proper cross-modal alignment.
AI.method: Combines frozen speech encoder and decoder-only language model via lightweight projection module, allowing structured context prompts (dialogue history, biasing words) to guide transcription. Employs contrastive learning objective to align speech and context representations in shared embedding space.
AI.result: Evaluated on over 1,500 hours of real-world conversational speech across 11 languages and 5 English dialects. Contextual input consistently improves recognition quality. Contrastive alignment provides additional gains across different context types, with overall performance gain exceeding 5%.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates importance of both contextual modeling and cross-modal alignment in multilingual ASR. The modular approach preserves pretrained model benefits while enabling effective multilingual context-aware speech recognition.

title: KCLarity at SemEval-2026 Task 6: Encoder and Zero-Shot Approaches to Political Evasion Detection
summary: This paper describes the KCLarity team's participation in CLARITY, a shared task at SemEval 2026 on classifying ambiguity and evasion techniques in political discourse. We investigate two modelling formulations: (i) directly predicting the clarity label, and (ii) predicting the evasion label and deriving clarity through the task taxonomy hierarchy. We further explore several auxiliary training variants and evaluate decoder-only models in a zero-shot setting under the evasion-first formulation. Overall, the two formulations yield comparable performance. Among encoder-based models, RoBERTa-large achieves the strongest results on the public test set, while zero-shot GPT-5.2 generalises better on the hidden evaluation set.

AI.tldr: KCLarity team's SemEval 2026 CLARITY task participation comparing direct clarity prediction vs. evasion-first hierarchical approach with RoBERTa-large and GPT-5.2 evaluations.
AI.motivation: To investigate effective modeling approaches for classifying ambiguity and evasion techniques in political discourse, comparing direct prediction of clarity labels versus hierarchical prediction through evasion labels.
AI.method: Two modeling formulations: (1) direct prediction of clarity label, (2) prediction of evasion label with clarity derived through task taxonomy hierarchy. Explored auxiliary training variants and evaluated decoder-only models in zero-shot setting under evasion-first formulation.
AI.result: Both formulations yielded comparable performance. RoBERTa-large achieved strongest results on public test set, while zero-shot GPT-5.2 generalized better on hidden evaluation set.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical evasion-first approach with zero-shot decoder models shows promising generalization capabilities, though encoder-based models perform better on standard test sets.
